content:
Hi, I use Vector Float 3, and I would like to write v.x instead of v[0] for notation.

In other languages like Scala / Kotlin there are "extension methods", where you can define your own methods onto pre-existing types that are not yours, i.e

extension (i : Int)
  def seconds = ...

3.seconds

extension (v : Vector Int)
  def x = v[0]

v.x  -- v[0]

does Lean have any facility for this?

Lean has what it calls "generalized field notation": when you write v.x, it looks at the type of v and looks for a function of the name x in the namespace with the name of the type of v. So you can do this:

import Std

abbrev Int.seconds (i : Int) : Std.Time.Second.Offset :=
  .ofInt i

#check (3 : Int).seconds -- Int.seconds 3 : Std.Time.Second.Offset

abbrev Vector.x (v : Vector Int 3) : Int :=
  v[0]

variable {v : Vector Int 3}

#check v.x  -- v.x : Int

You can find the details in the reference manual: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Terms/Function-Application/#generalized-field-notation

@Julia Markus Himmel Is it possible to extend the .x on multiple types of Vectors? I also want Vector Int 2 to have .x on it, but it says this is already defined for Vector Int 3 so there's a naming conflict.

you can add another parameter to generalize it

abbrev Vector.x {n : Nat} (v : Vector Int n) : Int :=...

Though in this specific case, the implementation is hard because this won't work for n = 0. A quick hack to make it compile again is

abbrev Vector.x (n : Nat) (v : Vector Int n) : Int :=
  v[0]! -- error if n = 0

But I suspect there is a better way
[NeZero n]?
or perhaps (hn : 0 < n := by get_elem_tac)

Lets say I choose tuples as the representation instead. A 3 dimensional vector is Float × Float × Float, a 2 dimensional vector is Float × Float. I can define

abbrev Prod.x : Float × Float × Float → Float := (·.fst)
abbrev Prod.y : Float × Float × Float → Float := (·.snd.fst)
abbrev Prod.z : Float × Float × Float → Float := (·.snd.snd)

But then I can no longer define the .x .y notation for 2D vectors Float × Float

abbrev Prod.x : Float × Float × Float → Float := (·.fst)
abbrev Prod.y : Float × Float × Float → Float := (·.snd.fst)
abbrev Prod.z : Float × Float × Float → Float := (·.snd.snd)

-- `Prod.x` has already been declaredLean 4
abbrev Prod.x : Float × Float → Float := (·.fst)
abbrev Prod.y : Float × Float → Float := (·.snd)
Or, If I wanted .r .g .b on tuples of 3 representing an rgb color, but also wanted .r .g .b .a on tuples of 4 representing an rgba color

(Yes I could use a structure, but I think tuples fit better and I prefer not to introduce nominal distinctions, I would like to be able to pass a color where a 3D position is expected for free, since they are truly equivalent structures.)
The problem here is .. × .. × .. × .. isn't a real n-tuple (even though it is isomorphic to one). So the moment I need to go above 2 dimension, I use either Fin n -> m for proof or Vector for program

Sorry why aren't product types real n-tuples? On the wiki for tuples I read

Tuples may be also defined from ordered pairs by a recurrence starting from an ordered pair; indeed, an n-tuple can be identified with the ordered pair of its (n − 1) first elements and its nth element, for example, (((1,2),3),4)=(1,2,3,4)

And in literature I often see physical coordinates as represented as Cartesian products, ℝ³ aka ℝ × ℝ × ℝ, which I can even define within Lean as notation

notation:max α "²" => α × α
notation:max α "³" => α × α × α

so ℝ³expands to ℝ × ℝ × ℝ. Looks like a very faithful implementation of the theory.
I mean, they are in the mathematical sense, but not in the programming sense

Do you just mean the ergonomics and cosmetics? We can define custom syntax .x .y .z and + Add * Mul typeclass instances for them to make them feel just as nice as any other construct for representing vectors. Is there any other issue with them?

Yeah, but it is also a little bit deeper than cosmetics

You can also see this problem in how wikipedia 's statement disagrees with Lean. Wikipedia is suggesting (1,2,3,4) = (((1,2),3),4), but Lean uses the convention (1,2,3,4) = (1,(2,(3,4)))

example :  (1,(2,(3,4))) = (1,2,3,4) := rfl

This kind of discrepancy suggests it is hard to make the × notation symmetrical and to mean a unique n-tuple type

I wonder if there is any Coe's or typelevel transformations we could do to make both of these true

example : (((1,2),3),4) = (1,2,3,4) := rfl
example : (((1,2),3),4) = (1,(2,(3,4))) := rfl
Anyway, it's not a dealbreaker for me, I still would like to use tuples in my video game. But getting the .x .y .z to work for both ℝ³ and ℝ² is giving me difficulty..
I assume this is some video game that happens in a 3D space that goes through traditional 3D rendering. What might soon annoy you more is multiplying matrix with α × α × α

Luckily I won't have to implement any of the 3D rendering logic, i'm at a layer right above that using bindings to a premade framework, and simply can wrap over it as an api. In the event that I ever do need to work with something closer to a real list, I can Coe ℝ³ (Vector ℝ 3) Coe (Vector ℝ 3) ℝ³ at that lower layer while still using tuples in my high level gameplay code.

Why does this not work?

class XAxis V where x : V → ℝ
class YAxis V where y : V → ℝ
class ZAxis V where z : V → ℝ

instance : XAxis ℝ³ where x := (·.fst)
instance : YAxis ℝ³ where y := (·.snd.fst)
instance : ZAxis ℝ³ where z := (·.snd.snd)

instance : XAxis ℝ² where x := (·.fst)
instance : YAxis ℝ² where y := (·.snd)

def v : ℝ³ := (1,1,1)
#check v.x -- Invalid field `x`: The environment does not contain `Prod.x`

Another solution is just to define your own structures for 3D and 2D tuples

structure Vec3 where
  x : Float
  y : Float
  z : Float
notation "ℝ³" => Vec3

structure Vec2 where
  x : Float
  y : Float
notation "ℝ²" => Vec2

def v1 : ℝ³ := ⟨3, 4, 5⟩
def v2 : ℝ² := ⟨7, 8⟩
def v3 : ℝ³ := {x := 2.4, y := 7.8, z := 9.2}

#eval v1.x
#eval v2.y
#eval v3.z

instance : YAxis ℝ³ where y := (·.snd.fst)
instance : ZAxis ℝ³ where z := (·.snd.snd)

I don't think dot notation supports this

Eric Paul said:

nother solution is just to define your own structures for 3D and 2D tuples

structure Vec3 where
  x : Float
  y : Float
  z : Float
notation "ℝ³" => Vec3

Yeah I thought of this, but a) then my general notation:max α "³" => α × α × α
notation won't work in the same file if I need some 3tuple of Floats in another context, like rgb colors, and b) it feels like I'm sort of lying at that point - pretending to use tuples instead of actually using tuples. α³ looks like an operation, that I expect to expand to α × α × α, but here users would realize it's just a cute cosmetic homage...

I feel that the lack of named tuples in the language does nerf them as a construct, since the answer is always "just use a structure instead".

Marvin said:

I feel that the lack of named tuples in the language does nerf them as a construct, since the answer is always "just use a structure instead".

What's the difference between a named tuple and a structure? In most languages it's that named tuples support accessing elements by both indexing and names, and that constructing them is possible with notation. But in Lean structures can do both of these as well. So what's the difference?

The big one that first comes to mind is that that named tuples can be defined (anonymously) and used immediately in the type-site, while structures require first defining the structure by name and then referencing it's name.

The next problem - though I think this is also true of most languages implementation of named tuples and wonder if there is some way to avoid this - is that structures introduce nominal type distinction - you cant pass an RGB value as a value for someone's position in the world, even though both are just 3 floats.
I would imagine treating RGB and XYZ the same is mostly useful in the render pipeline... but you also said that the 3D rendering logic is outside of Lean
So I don't quite understand the need of treating them the same
It's not so much about that specific use case, but that in general I think that's the right philosophy to have about data like this

I doubt that is the right philosophy at all. Continuing with this example, colors and positions, despite both having three components on the surface, have very different semantics. First of all, the popular color space is not linear
(even throwing out all the sRGB thing, at least I would argue that the color is a bounded space, while position is not)

Marvin said:

Yeah I thought of this, but a) then my general notation:max α "³" => α × α × α
notation won't work in the same file if I need some 3tuple of Floats in another context, like rgb colors, and ...

You can still use the general notation for different types as follows: 

structure Vec3 (α : Type) where
  x : α
  y : α
  z : α
notation α "³" => Vec3 α

structure Vec2 (α : Type) where
  x : α
  y : α
notation α "²" => Vec2 α

def v1 : Nat³ := ⟨3, 4, 5⟩
def v2 : String² := ⟨"hi", "bye"⟩
def v3 : Float³ := {x := 2.4, y := 7.8, z := 9.2}

#eval v1.x
#eval v2.y
#eval v3.z

Since both RGB and positions would be Float³, they could both be passed into the same places.

Marvin said:

The big one that first comes to mind is that that named tuples can be defined (anonymously) and used immediately in the type-site, while structures require first defining the structure by name and then referencing it's name.

It sounds like you're not talking about named tuples, but rather about either plain tuples or about dictionaries/hashmaps. Perhaps ordered dicts

Weiyi Wang said:

(even throwing out all the sRGB thing, at least I would argue that the color is a bounded space, while position is not)

Sure fair arguments. In general, how do you think we should decide when to think as data as nominally typed versus structurally typed? We both agree that we should not define distinct nominal types structure Position where x y z structure Velocity where x y z structure Acceleration where x y z and then coercions and operations between them when needed etc... Is it just "because you can to the same operations on them" that explains why we want them to be treated as the same type of thing?

Well, a derivative of a function 𝕜 → F is also a function 𝕜 → F (see docs#deriv), so this motivates position/velocity/acceleration being of the same type F. So it is kind of "do the same operations on them"

Eric Paul said:

Since both RGB and positions would be Float³, they could both be passed into the same places.

But then I would refer to an RGB only with .x .y .z, no way to say .r .g .b. I would like both .x and .r to be notations for the first value, if the notation is imported.

structure Vec3 where
  x : Float
  y : Float
  z : Float

def Vec3.r := Vec3.x
def Vec3.g := Vec3.y
def Vec3.b := Vec3.z

def myAwesomeVec3 : Vec3 := ⟨1, 2, 3⟩
#eval myAwesomeVec3.x
#eval myAwesomeVec3.y
#eval myAwesomeVec3.z
#eval myAwesomeVec3.r
#eval myAwesomeVec3.g
#eval myAwesomeVec3.b

You can also do this

class ProdGet (X : Type) (i : Nat) (Xi : outParam Type) where
  get : X → Xi

instance (priority:=low) : ProdGet X 0 X where
  get := fun x => x

instance : ProdGet (X×Y) 0 X where
  get := fun (x,_) => x

instance ha [ProdGet Y i Yi] : ProdGet (X×Y) (i+1) Yi where
  get := fun (_,y) => ProdGet.get i y

def Prod.x [ProdGet (X×Y) 0 X] (p : X×Y) : X := ProdGet.get 0 p
def Prod.y [ProdGet (X×Y) 1 Yi] (p : X×Y) : Yi := ProdGet.get 1 p
def Prod.z [ProdGet (X×Y) 2 Yi] (p : X×Y) : Yi := ProdGet.get 2 p
def Prod.r [ProdGet (X×Y) 0 X] (p : X×Y) : X := ProdGet.get 0 p
def Prod.g [ProdGet (X×Y) 1 Yi] (p : X×Y) : Yi := ProdGet.get 1 p
def Prod.b [ProdGet (X×Y) 2 Yi] (p : X×Y) : Yi := ProdGet.get 2 p

#eval (1,2,3).x
#eval (1,2,3).y
#eval (1,2,3).z
#eval (1,2,3).r
#eval (1,2,3).g
#eval (1,2,3).b
